newsitem.title: CANADA: Blizzard shuts down Winnipeg and Canada-U.S. border.
newsitem.headline: Blizzard shuts down Winnipeg and Canada-U.S. border.

text.p: Heavy snowfall and high winds sealed off the Canada-U.S. border overnight and brought this western Canadian city to a virtual standstill, officials said on Sunday.

"The blizzard started around 10 Saturday night and the snowfall should taper off by this evening but there's still going to be winds of up to 70 km per hour (45 mph)," Environment Canada meteorologist Henry Rymarczuk said.

U.S. I-29 in North Dakota and I-75 in Minnesota were closed at midnight Saturday while Manitoba Provincial Highway 75 remained open, Royal Canadian Mounted Police Const. Rob McCarthy said from the Emerson, Man., border crossing.

"I escorted one driver back to the detachment at midnight and I haven't been out since. We haven't closed the highway but it's been impassable since midnight. The snow drifts are about four to five feet high," McCarthy said.
About nine inches (20 cm) of snow fell in the Red River Valley by 0700 EST (1200 GMT) and about 12 inches (30 cm) in Kenora, Ontario, Rymarczuk said.
Manitoba's Highways Department urged motorists to stay off all roads including the TransCanada Highway and Hwy. 75.
Canadian National Railway Co and CP Rail System officials were not available for comment on the state of operations of their rail lines in western Canada.
"I haven't heard of any problems with the rail lines. The snow drifting's been pretty bad though," Canadian Wheat Board head of transportation John Benci said.

Winnipeg's 24-hour airport stayed open but only one flight had landed by early Sunday afternoon, a Twin-Otter bush plane, while a Northwest Airlines Corp flight was expected later in the afternoon, Winnipeg International Airport duty manager Brenda Belfry said.
